newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: FOCUS-Slovak trade gap growth seen set to resume.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Slovak trade gap growth seen set to resume.

text.p: Growth in Slovakia's foreign trade deficit slowed in June, but analysts said this was a short-term development rather than a reversal of the underlying negative trend.

The Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) said on Wednesday the trade gap widened to 32.57 billion crowns ($939.6 million) in the first half of 1997, up from a 29.62 billion shortfall in the first five months.
But the trade gap for June alone narrowed to 2.95 billion crowns, from 4.21 billion in May.
"The small deficit increase in June is better than was generally expected," said one foreign bank analyst.
"But it is certainly too early to celebrate any reversal of the trade trend, since the June slowdown was only a natural move after the rapid May deficit increase," the analyst said.
The deficit was likely to widen more rapidly later in the year, especially in the last quarter, he said.
Other analysts agreed, saying they saw little scope for any radical improvement of Slovakia's trade balance in coming months.

"I'm afraid the June figures do not indicate a longer-term improvement and there are several factors behind our expectations of a further widening of the trade deficit," said ING Barings' analyst Martin Barto.
An expected seasonal summer slowdown in industrial output and high interest rates were among the main factors expected to prevent any radical growth in exports, he said.
On the other hand, a large portion of unavoidable imports, such as raw materials, would prevent major cuts in imports.
Wednesday's data showed that cumulative imports rose 12.6 percent year-on-year to 177.33 billion crowns while exports rose 12.9 percent to 144.76 billion crowns.
Fossil fuels and mineral oils accounted for the largest portion of imports, rising 7.9 percent year-on-year to 31.22 billion crowns.
Technology imports, mainly equipment for upgrading the ageing Jaslovske Bohunice nuclear power plant and completing the Mochovce nuclear plant, also surged 20.2 percent to 28.29 billion crowns.
"The country will have to continue buying oil and gas abroad and will also have to keep up quite large technology imports for the Mochovce plant and the GSM network," said Barto.

Barto said foreign exchange developments would also influence Slovakia's trade balance since a large portion of imports was paid for in dollars. The full year deficit was likely to be higher than official forecasts, he said.
The government has said the 1997 trade gap should not exceed last year's shortfall of around 65 billion crowns, but some analysts foresee a deficit of between 70 and 75 billion crowns.
Economists said the widening of the June deficit, although slower than expected, also removed any chances for the central bank (NBS) to cut interest rates.
Since the middle of 1996, the NBS has been keeping monetary policy tight in order to curb consumer-oriented credit expansion which has fuelled growth in imports.
The NBS, in the face of pressure on the crown, moved further some two months ago and radically squeezed crown market liquidity. This pushed interbank rates above 20 percent.
"The NBS is not likely to ease its policy in the near future since its full year target of five percent of GDP seems unreachable," Barto said.
-- Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-521-8402 ($ = 34.66 Slovak Crowns)
